classical

Sall. Cat. 54.2: ille mānsuētūdine et misericordiā clārus factus, huic sevēritās dignitātem addiderat

ille, illa, illud

pronoun · Declension on Wiktionary

the former (with hic, the latter)

Hic, “this one”, points to the nearer of two, so usually the latter; ille, “that one”, to the farther, the former. But Latin goes by thought, not by word order: hic can be the one that matters more to the speaker, even if it was named first (Cic. Lael. 10; Lewis & Short, s.v. ille).

Other words

  • prior, prius — the former, the first of two (in time or order)

    adjective (comparative); its pair is posterior · also used · classical · Cic. Ac. 2.44: ita priōrī posterius, posteriōrī superius nōn jungitur (Lewis & Short); Cic. Fam. 1.9.24: priōre aestāte, the summer before (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Cicero sets prior against posterior, and says superior for “former” in relation to the present (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Caesar beneficiīs ac mūnificentiā magnus habēbātur, integritāte vītae Catō. ille mānsuētūdine et misericordiā clārus factus, huic sevēritās dignitātem addiderat

    Caesar was thought great for his kindnesses and his generosity, Cato for the integrity of his life. The former had won fame by his gentleness and mercy; the latter’s strictness had added to his standingSall. Cat. 54.2

  • illīus facilitās, hujus cōnstantia laudābātur

    the former was praised for his easy kindness, the latter for his firmnessSall. Cat. 54.3

See also former, last.
